synopsis: The manufacturer is developing automatic braking that intervenes if the operator does not react, so validation still requires assumptions about operator actions and intervention waiting time [f2955, f11484, f11821]. No representative field-measured distribution of heavy-machine operators’ responses to proximity warnings, or validated off-road operator model, was found; the booklet recommends uncertain response parameters and sensitivity analysis rather than a validated average [f11814, f3040, f11822]. Borrowed road-research delays are 0.5–1 s, while the broader cited assumptions span approximately 0.5–2.5 s and a Hitachi patent allows a 1–3 s margin; the illustrative combined operator-plus-mechanical delay of 2 s adds 22.2 m of travel at 40 km/h before braking distance [f3017, f6228, f6206, f3220]. ISO 3450:2011 excludes operator reaction from stopping distance, whereas US MSHA Table M-1 includes 1 s of operator time plus 0.5–2.5 s of system response; the corpus also says ISO 21815-3 both excludes operator time from stopping distance and accounts for operator action time, leaving the distinction insufficiently explained [f5976, f6058, f2898, f6241]. Machine simulators can establish responses to warnings, and warning-fleet history may anchor response timing, but behaviour under automatic braking may differ from warning-only behaviour [f960, f7931, f7479]. Human-machine interface timing and warning-zone extent must provide response opportunity, and driver-model choice materially affects predicted benefit: cited road research estimates warning-system benefits of 53–96% [f11843, f13901, f3045].
